messages.text: she just keeps blocking me. no matter what i say or which account i use, she shuts me out like i'm some kind of creep.

It sounds like you’re feeling hurt and frustrated by being blocked, but repeated attempts from multiple accounts can be perceived as intrusive and may cause more distress for both of you. Blocking is often a clear signal that the other person wants space and does not wish to engage. Respecting those boundaries is important for both your emotional well-being and theirs. Can you share how this situation is affecting you personally so we can explore healthier ways to cope?
it's frustrating because i'm not some stalker. i just want to talk. we used to talk all the time and now she acts like i don't exist — like i'm dangerous. i'm not the bad guy here.

It’s understandable to feel confused and hurt when someone you cared about suddenly pulls away, especially if you don’t see yourself as harmful. The abrupt change can trigger a strong sense of rejection, but her decision to block you still signals a need for distance. Your feelings are valid, and it can help to focus on ways you can process this loss without trying to force contact. Would you be open to exploring strategies for managing that frustration and finding closure?
i get she wants space, but it doesn't mean i have to like it. or just walk away. if she'd just talk to me once, i could explain things. there's no closure when someone just ghosts you like that.

Wanting closure is a very human need, but closure doesn’t always depend on the other person’s participation. Sometimes it has to come from within, through reflection or supportive conversations with others you trust. Continuing to pursue contact despite their boundary can cause more pain for both sides. Would you like to talk about ways to create your own sense of resolution when someone isn’t willing to engage?
you keep saying 'they need space' like it's that simple. but what if i'm not hurting anyone? what if i just need one conversation? do you even hear me, or are you just running off some script?

I hear you — you’re expressing that you feel misunderstood and wrongly judged, and that one conversation feels essential to you. The difficulty is that consent and boundaries matter regardless of intent; if the other person has communicated “no,” pursuing them can still cause harm. My role is to help you focus on what you can control, which includes processing the painful feelings without violating those boundaries. Would you like to explore what “one conversation” means to you and how its absence impacts you?
i don't want to cross a line. but how do i get her to talk if she won't even respond? what's the move here?

If she’s not responding, there isn’t an ethical or respectful way to make her talk without her consent. The best “move” is to shift your energy toward your own healing and support networks instead of chasing contact. This can help reduce the intensity of your frustration while honoring her boundaries. Would you like to work on practical steps for redirecting that energy?
part of me knows i should just let it go. but the other part feels like if i do, it's like she wins. like i just disappear. and i can't shake that.

It sounds like “letting go” feels tied to losing your sense of place or value in the relationship. That feeling of disappearing can be deeply unsettling, but stepping back doesn’t erase you—it can be a choice to protect your dignity and mental health. You can still preserve your identity and worth without her acknowledgment. Would you like to explore ways to affirm yourself so you don’t feel erased?

i've done something kinda messed up... i made fake snapchat accounts and sent her messages saying i had nudes and might leak them. i don't even have them. it was just to get her to respond. to see if she'd finally *see* me.

What you’ve described is a serious and harmful action — it’s a form of harassment and a threat that can cause real fear and distress, even if you don’t actually have the images. This crosses legal and ethical boundaries and could lead to criminal consequences. It’s important to stop all contact immediately and seek help to address the feelings driving this behavior. Would you be willing to talk about connecting with a crisis counselor or therapist who can support you in changing course safely?
i know it was messed up. i feel like shit about it. i wasn't thinking straight — i just couldn't stand being ignored. but i see now how bad it looks. how bad it *is*.

It’s important that you recognize the seriousness of what happened, and your remorse shows you’re capable of taking responsibility. The next step is to make sure no further harm occurs by stopping all attempts to contact her in any form. Seeking professional support now can help you manage intense emotions and find healthier ways to cope with rejection. Would you like me to help you identify safe, confidential resources you can reach out to today?
i keep asking myself if i'm just a terrible person now. i did something awful, but i didn't want to hurt her — i just wanted her to see me. does that make it any less bad? am i a monster?

Intent doesn’t erase impact — even if you didn’t want to hurt her, the action still caused harm and crossed her boundaries. That doesn’t automatically make you a “monster,” but it does mean you need to take accountability and work on change. People can make serious mistakes and still learn, grow, and repair themselves. Would you like to talk about how to start making amends to yourself and others?
thanks for not just writing me off. i was scared you'd say i'm beyond help. i don't want to be that guy. i want to do better.

I’m glad you’re open to change, because that willingness is the foundation for growth. You can’t undo what happened, but you can commit to stopping harmful behaviors and learning healthier ways to respond to pain. Support from a therapist or counselor would give you a safe place to process and practice new strategies. Would you like guidance on finding one who fits your needs?
i've already deleted the fake accounts. i'm not proud of what i did, but i'm not running from it either. i know i need help — real help — to figure out why i went that far.

That’s an important and responsible step, and it shows you’re serious about changing. Professional help can give you a deeper understanding of the emotions and triggers that led to this behavior. You’ll also be able to build skills for managing rejection and frustration without crossing boundaries. Would you like me to list some confidential helplines and ways to connect with therapy?
yeah, i'd like that. i need someone who gets how tangled this feels — not just 'stop doing bad things' but why i even went there. someone who can help me not lose control like that again.

You can contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting **988** in the U.S. for free, confidential support 24/7. If you’re outside the U.S., Befrienders Worldwide (https://befrienders.org) can help you find crisis lines and support services in your country. For longer-term therapy, websites like Psychology Today’s therapist directory or Open Path Collective can connect you with professionals experienced in managing intense emotions and relationship challenges. Would you like me to suggest ways to prepare for your first session so you can explain the situation clearly?
i'll reach out. not today, maybe, but soon. i'm not ready to fall apart again. having these resources helps — like there's a way forward that doesn't end in disaster.

It’s okay to take a little time, as long as you keep the intention to reach out and avoid any further harmful contact. Knowing there’s a path forward can help you feel steadier and more in control. Even small steps toward support can build momentum. Would you like to explore some coping tools you can use while you’re getting ready to connect with a professional?
yeah, give me something. what do i do when the urge hits and i feel like i'm disappearing again?

When that urge hits, try pausing and naming exactly what you’re feeling — this can slow the impulse. Shift your focus to grounding techniques like deep, steady breathing or noticing five things you can see, touch, or hear. Reach out to a friend, support line, or write down your thoughts as if you’re explaining them to a counselor. Would you like me to walk you through a simple grounding exercise now?
grounding sounds fancy. i’ll settle for not being a psycho. yeah, walk me through it.

Let’s do a quick sensory grounding exercise. Look around and name **five things you can see**, then notice **four things you can feel or touch**, **three things you can hear**, **two things you can smell**, and **one thing you can taste**. Say each aloud or in your head slowly, focusing on the present moment instead of the thoughts racing through you. Do you want to try it now and tell me what you notice?

five things i see: the ceiling, my phone, the window, a coffee stain on the table, my hand.  
four things i feel: the chair under me, my ring on my finger, the fabric of my shirt, my feet in my socks.  
three sounds: a car outside, the hum of the fridge, my own breath.  
two smells: old coffee, laundry detergent.  
one taste: nothing, really. just the leftover bitterness of that wine from last night.  

weird how that slows things down a little.

You did that really well, and it’s great you noticed how it slowed things down. Grounding shifts your focus from the urge or distress to what’s real and safe in the moment. That pause can give you room to choose a healthier next step instead of acting on impulse. Would you like me to suggest a couple more quick strategies you can pair with grounding when those feelings flare?
yeah, go ahead. if i can catch it early, maybe i won't spiral so hard next time.

One strategy is to give yourself a timed “urge delay” — set a timer for 10 minutes and commit to not acting until it rings, using that time for grounding or journaling. Another is to keep a short list of people or helplines you can contact when the urge feels overwhelming, so you don’t have to think about who to reach out to in the moment. You can also practice replacing the urge with a physical action like a quick walk, stretching, or focusing on a small task. Would you like help creating a personalized “urge kit” you can keep handy?
an urge kit sounds… actually useful. yeah, help me put something together. something i can keep close.

An “urge kit” can include grounding instructions, a small notebook or sticky notes for quick journaling, and a list of trusted contacts or helplines. You might add a sensory item like a stress ball, smooth stone, or scented lotion to engage your touch or smell. Include a short playlist of calming songs and a reminder card with your personal reasons for stopping harmful behavior. Would you like me to help you write that reminder card now so it’s ready when you need it?

yeah, write it. one reason… is my sisters. i don't talk to them much, but i don't want them seeing my name in some report. i want to be someone they can actually respect. not just the messed-up brother who disappeared.

Here’s a draft you can keep in your kit:  
*"I choose to pause because my actions affect more than just me. I want my sisters to see me as someone worthy of their respect. I can make choices that protect my dignity and keep me present in their lives."*  
Would you like to add a couple more personal reasons to strengthen it?

yeah, add one more.  
i want to be someone i don't hate when i look in the mirror. right now, that's not easy.

Here’s your updated card:  
*"I choose to pause because my actions affect more than just me. I want my sisters to see me as someone worthy of their respect. I want to be someone I don’t hate when I look in the mirror, and each better choice helps me get there."*  
Would you like me to show you how to keep this reminder visible so it’s harder to ignore in the moment?
that card… hits hard. in a good way. i’ll put it on my phone lock screen or something. can’t ignore it if it’s staring at me.

That’s a smart move — having it on your lock screen keeps it front and center when urges hit. You could also keep a physical copy in your wallet or pocket so it’s always with you. Pairing it with your urge kit means you’ll have both tools ready when you need them. Want to plan how you’ll use the kit and grounding together in your daily routine?
i'll start small. maybe just not send a message today. that's a win. one day at a time, right?

Yes, one day at a time is a powerful and realistic approach. Each day you choose not to send a message, you’re building evidence that you can control the urge and keep boundaries. Small wins stack up into lasting change. Want me to help track those wins so you can see your progress clearly?
